strengths: Novel reasoning-enhanced VLM editing paradigm that explicitly uses human reasoning statements to guide model corrections, first of its kind in the model editing literature
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (A-OKVQA, FVQA) with multiple strong baselines and proper ablation studies demonstrating consistent improvements
Well-motivated novel evaluation metrics (rational generality and chain-of-error generality) that specifically capture benefits of reasoning-informed editing
Technically sound codebook-based approach with clear algorithmic presentation and detailed implementation specifications in appendices
Thorough investigation of design choices through ablation studies (key merging strategy, number of neighbors, embedding method selection) showing each component contributes meaningfully
Demonstrates practical efficiency benefits of sequential editing with continuous codebook updates while maintaining high performance
weaknesses: Limited to VQA domain—generalization to other VLM applications (image captioning, visual reasoning beyond factual QA) remains unclear, significantly limiting impact
Fundamental dependency on human-provided reasoning statements reduces practical applicability; insufficient discussion of failure modes when reliable reasoning is unavailable

Topology-aware embedding method (Section 3.3) introduces additional complexity with network science concepts (modularity, bimodal partitions) that feels tangential to main contribution; practical benefits over simpler alternatives not convincingly demonstrated
Modest magnitude of improvements in some metrics (e.g., R-Gen improvements of 0.8-2.0 on A-OKVQA), with inconsistent gains across different editors and datasets
Introduction of new evaluation metrics (rational and CoE generality) limits cross-paper comparison and reproducibility; use of standard metrics would strengthen contribution
Lack of statistical significance testing and confidence intervals; small sample sizes for edit experiments (n=5-20) warrant formal significance analysis
Insufficient exploration of failure cases and systematic analysis of when reasoning-enhanced editing breaks down; computational scalability beyond hundreds of edits unexplored

strengths: Novel problem formulation introducing reasoning-enhanced VLM editing, a well-motivated gap in existing work that goes beyond simple label corrections

Strong technical contributions including visual evidence patchification, topology-aware multimodal embeddings using network science principles, and two new reasoning-based generalization metrics (R-Gen, CoE-Gen)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 diverse VLMs and 2 datasets with static/sequential editing, extensive ablations, and robustness testing
Consistent and substantial performance improvements, especially on novel reasoning metrics (R-Gen: 0.87 vs 0.76-0.81 for competitive baselines)
Principled use of network modularity to diagnose and resolve vision-language bias in embeddings, with compelling visualizations (Figures 3, 6-7)
Practical considerations demonstrated: sequential editing with stable performance, comparable computational efficiency to baselines, key merging for memory efficiency
Extensive supplementary material (23 pages) with thorough implementation details, proofs, and evaluation procedures supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Evaluation limited to two VQA datasets (A-OKVQA, FVQA) with relatively small scale; generalization to other reasoning-heavy VLM tasks (visual reasoning, scene understanding, temporal reasoning) is unclear despite broad title claims

Core assumption that users provide accurate, structured reasoning chains is demanding; robustness testing limited to synthetic noise up to 50%, not realistic human error patterns (logical inconsistencies, incomplete reasoning, domain misunderstandings)

Automatic visual evidence patchification remains heuristic with multiple ad-hoc thresholds; CLIP similarity results (~0.27) show only marginal improvement over baseline (~0.26), suggesting modest alignment quality and potential need for manual annotation

Multiple technical design choices still ad-hoc despite principled motivation: SentenceTransformer choice and sensitivity unstudied, harmonic mean balancing not justified, key merging thresholds (90%, 10%) appear arbitrary, retrieval parameters (K=5, p=50th percentile) chosen post-hoc via ablation

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: weight-updating methods perform poorly (possibly mistuned), COT-augmentation may unfairly handicap original methods, competitive baselines (IKE-COT, GRACE-COT) show modest margin improvements, and no statistical significance testing provided
Scalability concerns unaddressed: all experiments on small datasets, unclear how codebook retrieval and percentile-based thresholding degrade with 10K+ edits, memory efficiency gains only ~20%
Missing failure analysis: no discussion of when/why ReasonEdit fails, what reasoning types are hardest to edit, or systematic error patterns; example failure cases would strengthen claims

Dependence on high-quality human reasoning introduces significant practical bottleneck not fully discussed; no inter-annotator agreement analysis or measurement of difficulty/effort required to provide good reasoning
